title: Is legal tech funding losing steam? We checked the numbers.
excerpt: Legal-tech startups, including Harvey and Legora, raised a record $4.6 billion in 2025, but funding has not kept up this year.
content_html:
2026-11-16T15:00:22.324Z

I’m heading to Scottsdale for the TLTF Summit, an invite-only gathering of law firm leaders, general counsels, and startup builders, with one question: Is winter coming for legal tech?

Mentioned in this issue: Victor Wang, Eilla, Crunchbase, Harvey, Legora, Anthropic, Davis Polk, Nikki Shaver, Leah, Latham & Watkins, Crosby, Norm, Atticus, Finch, Theo Ai, Irys, Eve, Jay Madheswaran, Emily Heyward, Red Antler, Laurel, and Ryan Alshak. 

Agenda

  • Funding for legal tech takes a sharp turn
  • What I’m reading and writing
  • Legal tech’s very human names

Legal tech’s haves and have-nots

A LinkedIn post from commercial lawyer Victor Wang caught my attention last week.

Wang cited data from startup Eilla suggesting that funding for legal-tech startups fell 39% year over year after stripping out the blockbuster rounds for Harvey and Legora.

I decided to check Eilla’s math against Crunchbase, a database I use regularly.

Crunchbase shows that legal-tech startups raised a record $4.6 billion in 2025. Harvey and Legora’s rounds alone accounted for just over $1 billion, or 23% of that total.

So far this year, startups in the space have raised $3.8 billion, per Crunchbase. The two giants took a bigger share. Their rounds account for $1.95 billion, or 51% of all funding.

So, how does Eilla’s thesis hold up?

Crunchbase suggests the gap may be even wider. Funding for everyone else totals $1.89 billion so far this year, compared with $3.59 billion in all of 2025 — a difference of roughly 47%.

One important caveat: This compares a year-to-date figure with a full-year total. Still, the concentration of capital is hard to miss — and the drop-off hard to ignore.

Two plausible explanations:

The category is maturing. Investors may see Harvey and Legora as the runaway leaders in the race for law firms and corporate legal departments. Those who can get in may prefer to write larger checks to the two companies rather than spread their bets across younger startups.

Investors may also be waiting to see how the model labs change the game. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Microsoft are all moving deeper into the legal market. That could make investors wary of startups that look like thin wrappers around the same underlying models.

I’ll be looking for other explanations at the TLTF Summit. Tell me your theories.

Quick links

  • Anthropic’s IPO offers law firms a chance to share in the windfall. (Business Insider)
  • Davis Polk has hired Nikki Shaver as the firm’s first chief AI officer. (Reuters)
  • AI-native law firm Crosby has secured a $5 million malpractice insurance policy for its AI agents. (The New York Times)
  • Latham & Watkins has budgeted $1 million in 2027 for rewarding associates who “lead or materially contribute to AI initiatives.” (Reuters)

Why do so many legal-tech startups have human names?

Now that I’ve said it, you can’t unsee it: An astonishing number of startups building for lawyers have human names.

There’s Harvey, named partly for “Suits” superlawyer Harvey Specter. Legora was once Leya, not to be confused with contracts startup Leah. Crosby and Norm sound like two guys from the Rat Pack. Legal tech has room for not one but two companies named Atticus, plus a Finch.

For an industry obsessed with automating human work, its startups seem awfully attached to names you’d find on a Park Slope preschool roster. Looking at you, Theo Ai and Irys.

For centuries, law firms have been putting people’s names on the door, trading on the reputations of the lawyers behind them. The startups may be following suit.

Eve makes software for plaintiff-side firms that help everyday people take on insurers and corporations. Cofounder Jay Madheswaran says the company takes its name from EVE, the sleek robot who steals WALL-E’s heart in the Pixar movie, not the biblical first woman.

“EVE plays a very heroic role and we felt that was appropriate,” he said. “Also, we’re big fans of palindromes.”

Emily Heyward has another theory. Her branding agency, Red Antler, worked with Laurel, a startup that helps lawyers track their billable hours, when it rebranded from Time by Ping.

Human names took off during consumer tech’s heyday, as startups like Casper and Oscar were trying to persuade people to do unfamiliar things online, like buy a mattress or shop for health insurance. Now, legal tech is asking lawyers to trust machines with work once done by people.

Heyward thinks a friendly name can help make that leap feel a little less daunting. “It’s like a business you could grab a beer with,” she said.

For Ryan Alshak, cofounder of Laurel, the name checked a few boxes. It has roots in ancient Greece, where laurel wreaths symbolized victory and honor. He also liked that it began and ended with the same letter, “to symbolize that time is both finite and infinite,” he said.

The name turned out to be more personal than he imagined.

Earlier this year, Alshak got curious about the meaning of his late mother’s name. Randa, he discovered, is an Arabic name associated with a fragrant tree: the bay laurel.

“Sometimes the name chooses us,” he said.

For an industry obsessed with automating human work, its startups seem awfully attached to names you’d find on a Park Slope preschool roster. Looking at you, Theo Ai and Irys.

For centuries, law firms have been putting people’s names on the door, trading on the reputations of the lawyers behind them. The startups may be following suit.

Eve makes software for plaintiff-side firms that help everyday people take on insurers and corporations. Cofounder Jay Madheswaran says the company takes its name from EVE, the sleek robot who steals WALL-E’s heart in the Pixar movie, not the biblical first woman.

“EVE plays a very heroic role and we felt that was appropriate,” he said. “Also, we’re big fans of palindromes.”

Emily Heyward has another theory. Her branding agency, Red Antler, worked with Laurel, a startup that helps lawyers track their billable hours, when it rebranded from Time by Ping.

Human names took off during consumer tech’s heyday, as startups like Casper and Oscar were trying to persuade people to do unfamiliar things online, like buy a mattress or shop for health insurance. Now, legal tech is asking lawyers to trust machines with work once done by people.

Heyward thinks a friendly name can help make that leap feel a little less daunting. “It’s like a business you could grab a beer with,” she said.

For Ryan Alshak, cofounder of Laurel, the name checked a few boxes. It has roots in ancient Greece, where laurel wreaths symbolized victory and honor. He also liked that it began and ended with the same letter, “to symbolize that time is both finite and infinite,” he said.

The name turned out to be more personal than he imagined.

Earlier this year, Alshak got curious about the meaning of his late mother’s name. Randa, he discovered, is an Arabic name associated with a fragrant tree: the bay laurel.

“Sometimes the name chooses us,” he said.
